**[p. 185]** Surah 98, Lam Yakun, also called al-Qiyama and al-Munfakkin.

Its purpose is to inform that this upright Book, by the loftiness of its station and the greatness of its effects, is, just as it is a light and guidance for one people, a deafness and blindness for others. It leads to Paradise, the abode of the righteous, and drives to the Fire, the abode of the wretched sinners. This is indicated by each of its names, "Those who disbelieve" and "the Munfakkin," through reflection on the verse's division of people into the wretched and the happy. [It is indicated] by "In the name of Allah," who has absolute exaltedness, so nothing escapes His will; by "the Most Merciful," who encompassed all His servants with the blessing of bringing them into existence and making clear to them; and by "the Most Merciful," who singled out the people of His love with righteous deeds, which are burdensome, by saving their doers and making them happy.

* *

When Allah, glorified and exalted, informed that the blessed night, which He protected with a kind of concealment, both in the descent of those who descend in it and in its specific identification, will continue to exist with that quality until dawn arrives, by which the complete clarity is achieved, He informed that the people of religions, whether a religion had a root in truth or not, would not, under the customary course of wisdom in the causes within the abode of causes, shift from what they are in except through a great cause **[p. 186]** whose clarity is greater than the clarity of dawn. This is the Qur'an, mentioned in the context of the Decree, and the Messenger to whom it was sent down. So He said: ﴿Had not been﴾, meaning in absolute time, past, present and future, as a nature and disposition. This indicates what they were upon before that: that they would exchange what they were upon of disbelief or faith for disbelief or innovation, and then would not remain firm upon it, because that is not in their natures, but is a passing, transient impulse, as is related of their conduct after Moses, peace be upon him, [when the prophets were governing them, peace be upon them]. This is indicated in part by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They became blind and deaf; then Allah turned to them; then many of them became blind and deaf again﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 71]. Likewise the polytheists used to alter the religion of Ismail, peace be upon him, yet they did not wholly separate from it. At times they worshipped idols, at times the angels, and at other times the jinn. They did not remain upon one state with complete steadfastness, like their steadfastness upon Islam after the coming of the clear proof and their complete forgetting of the matters of the Jahiliyya, to the point that they forgot the maysir (gambling), so that none of their children knew its manner; and likewise the sa'iba (freed camel) and what accompanied it, and other such superstitions of theirs. ﴿Those who disbelieve﴾, meaning whether they were deeply rooted in disbelief or not.

Since the world is more deserving of following the truth and more grievous in guilt when committing what calls for blame, He began with His saying: ﴿from the People of the Book﴾, meaning from the Jews and the Christians, whose original religion was true, but they deviated from it by alteration, distortion and crookedness **[p. 187]** concerning the attributes of Allah, exalted is He. Then Allah abrogated it (naskh) by what He legislated, by differing from it in the subsidiary matters (furu') and agreeing with it in the fundamentals (usul). So they denied. ﴿And the polytheists﴾, meaning by worshipping idols, fire, the sun, and the like, from those who were deeply rooted in a religion that had no root in the truth, in that they had no Book. ﴿Munfakkin﴾, meaning separated and departing from what they were upon of their religion, with a separation that removes them from it completely, such that no bond with it remains for them, and they remain firm upon that separation. The root of fakk is opening and separation, when something was joined together, as in fakk al-kitab (unsealing a book), al-khatm (the seal), and al-'azm (the bone), when it parts from what was adhering and connected to it. Or [it means separation] from what is in their souls of the supposition of following the truth when the Messenger announced in advance comes to them, as the People of the Book used to seek victory through him, and the polytheists used to swear by Allah with their most earnest oaths: ﴿If a warner came to them, they would surely be better guided than any other nation﴾ [Fatir: 42]. Thus they would become by that factions and sects. ﴿Until﴾, meaning up to the point that ﴿there comes to them﴾, He used the present tense to indicate the renewal of the clear proof at every time, through the renewal of the message and the recitation. ﴿The clear proof﴾, meaning the sign which in clarity is like the shining dawn, which does not increase with the passage of time except in manifestness, radiance and light. That is the Messenger and the signs with him, the greatest of which is the Book, whether it be the Torah, the Gospel, the Psalms **[p. 188]** or the Furqan (the Criterion). For this reason, He substituted from it by His saying:

Here is the translation:

﴿A messenger﴾, i.e., one of great stature, and he increased his greatness by describing him with the words: ﴿from Allah﴾, [i.e.,] the One who possesses majesty and honor. ﴿Reciting﴾, i.e., reading, in a continuous, widely transmitted recitation, is that Messenger, after Our teaching him, ﴿pages﴾, the plural of ṣaḥīfah (page), which is a sheet of paper, and what is meant is what is in them; he used the word for them to refer to him because of the intensity of their connection. ﴿Purified﴾, i.e., they are in the utmost state of purity, cleanliness, and freedom from every impurity, by what We have placed in them of distance from filth, in that falsehood, including the associating of idols and other things with Allah, and every deviation, does not come to them from before them or from behind them, and that none touches them except the purified. And his recitation of them, even though he is unlettered, is a recitation of what is in them.

When he had magnified it by describing its scrolls, which are the place where the writings are inscribed, as purified, he explained the reason for that, saying: ﴿Therein are [true] books﴾, meaning those scrolls contain ﴿books﴾, the plural of kitab, that is, sciences which, because of their preciousness, truly deserve to be written, ﴿upright﴾, meaning they are in the utmost rectitude, because they speak the truth about which there is no doubt, and there is in them no polytheism and no crookedness of any kind. So when this clear proof came to them, they separated. Their separation shows that they had been united before this: the People of the Book believed in the Prophet ﷺ because of the explicit good tidings about him that they had, while the polytheists were saying: ﴿If a warner came to us, we would surely be better guided than any of the [other] nations﴾, and they were saying: "We know the truth and its people, and we will not reject it in any way." But when the Prophet ﷺ came to them with what has no ambiguity, they split: some of them believed and some of them disbelieved.

Imam Abu Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr said: This [verse] is part of the perfection of what precedes it. When He commanded him, upon him be blessings and peace, to recite His Book, through which his path became clear and his proof was established, and then followed that with a description of the night of its revelation and the magnifying of that night by magnifying what it was made fit for, of what was sent down in it, He followed that with informing him ﷺ that this Book is the one through which the Jews used to seek victory over the polytheists of the Arabs, and they used to glorify its matter and the matter of the one who would bring it. Then, when that became visible to them, they became the first to disbelieve in it. So He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Those who disbelieved among the People of the Book and the polytheists were not going to separate until there came to them the clear proof﴾ [al-Bayyinah: 1], up to His saying: ﴿And that is the upright religion﴾ [al-Bayyinah: 5]. In informing about this there is an emphasis on what has been explained before, which produces fear and leads, by God's permission, to submission and to disavowing the claim of any power or strength. For these people had been warned about the matter of the Book and the one who would bring it; they would find him written among them in the Torah and the Gospel. They had been hoping to be victorious through him, upon him be blessings and peace, over their enemies, and they used to seek victory through his Book. So may God have mercy on the one who had no knowledge of it, like Abu Bakr and Umar and their likes, may God be pleased with them all. And He made forbidden for those who had been upon insight into His matter and made them, by their disbelief, the worst of creatures. He was pleased with the others and they were pleased with Him, and He housed them in His neighborhood and granted them the great triumph and eternal life, even though they were before his mission, upon him be blessings and peace, in ignorance and blindness. Since what had already preceded for them in eternity, ﴿Those are the best of creatures﴾, did not harm them. End.

Since the expression was: "When it comes to them, they separate." Indeed, the polytheists split after your coming, and the Great Proof came to them, some guided and some astray, and the astray ones were some openly defiant and some concealing. So too were the People of the Book. Then [what] the Arabs gathered upon guidance was only after the Proof had come to them. He conjoined to this, which the context had conveyed, his saying, informing of the increased ugliness in the commission of sin by the world by singling them out explicitly from the polytheists: ﴿And those who were given the Book did not split﴾, meaning now and in the past of time, a great splitting ﴿...those who were given the Book﴾. And since they were in a state that is more fitting for turning away, he put the verb in the passive, [saying] ﴿were given the Book﴾, meaning, from what they were upon of consensus on error, or the promise to follow the awaited truth concerning Muhammad (ﷺ). Likewise was their conduct toward 'Isa (ﷺ) before. Some of them persisted in error and went to extremes in breaking the covenant and in obstinacy, while some fulfilled the promise and were guided. Their splitting did not become a split except for a short time. Then they gathered, and among them none was secured who would count their successor's [position] for those remaining as a split, because it was a little out of much. Therefore he introduced the preposition, saying: ﴿except after﴾. That short time was the conversion of those tribes of the Arabs who had consensually adhered to Christianity, such as Tanukh, Ghassan, 'Amilah, Bakr ibn Wa'il, 'Abd al-Qays and their like, and likewise those from the tribes of Yemen who had become Jewish and then embraced Islam. Then the Jews and Christians consensually adhered to error, and none from it embraced Islam except those who, because of their small number, would not count as dividers of them. ﴿what﴾, meaning the time in which ﴿the Proof came to them﴾, or the coming of ﴿the Clear Proof﴾ in it. So their state was as He, glorified is He, said: ﴿And previously they used to seek victory over those who disbelieved, but when there came to them what they recognized, they disbelieved in it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 89]. The coming of the Proof required their gathering upon the truth, not their splitting over it. It seems he alluded to the polytheists by the conjunction, without explicitly mentioning them, because they were the reverse of the People of the Book: they did not split except for a short time at the beginning of the matter, so the astray among them were more numerous. Then they consensually adhered to guidance, owing to their upright natures and balanced temperaments. That indicates the utmost crookedness of the People of the Book, because they, given the knowledge they possessed, were more deserving than the polytheists of gathering upon guidance. It also indicates that the occurrence of obstinacy and stubbornness is more frequent among the learned, and that the calamity that befalls them comes from the strength of the turbidity of the deficiency in their natures, nurtured and developed [p-192] by sins, such as consuming illicit gain through usury and other major sins, and procrastinating repentance. Their bodies grew accustomed to that, and their hearts became saturated with it, until their darkness piled up and their rust and cloud became dense. So when they were called, there was nothing in them of light by which they would have readiness to submit to the call.

**(Al-Biqa'i, Nazm al-Durar, on Surah 98, verse 5)**

Since the state of those who went astray while possessing knowledge is more shameful, He increased their disgrace, saying: ﴿And they were not﴾, meaning: they did that while the situation was that they were not [commanded otherwise]. Since the intended point is the manifestation of the matter that is obeyed, and not the identity of the one who commands, He said, after describing the scriptures as having been established as "qayyimah" (upright), with the verb built for the passive: ﴿They were commanded﴾, meaning: their command occurred with what they were commanded, from the One who, when the command is stated without qualification, deserves that it be understood only as coming from Him, in those books whose following is obligatory and to which they submitted [to Him]: ﴿except to worship﴾, meaning: in order that they worship ﴿Allah﴾, meaning the God to whom all command belongs and to whom no one else has any command, by bringing about His worship and renewing it at every time. Worship (*ibadah*) is the execution of Allah the Exalted's command as He commanded it, in the manner commanded, because He is the Commander, together with hastening to it with the utmost love, humility and glorification. This is to be done with moderation, lest the person become bored and thus fall short, or become self-admiring so that his worship is corrupted. Their state is that they are ﴿sincere﴾, meaning their sincerity is firmly established to the utmost degree, ﴿in religion for Him﴾, in such a way that there is no admixture in it of anything that clouds it, whether manifest or hidden polytheism (*shirk*), such that (p-193) the obedience is for the sake of His being the One who commanded it, pleasing Him, and not for any benefit or harm. And this must be upon correctness, for many of those who act sincerely build on a foundation that is not sound, so it does not benefit them but becomes a burden upon them, because they have neglected the root, like the monks. Likewise many who believe in the sainthood of a person while not knowing how to distinguish between the friend of Allah and the enemy, or between one who is honored and one who is being led on gradually. The reality of sincerity (*ikhlas*) is that it is singling out the Truth in obedience by intention, together with forgetting creation in deeds, and reaching Him by guarding against being observed by people, together with purifying oneself from watching the self, by the servant seeing himself as a servant who is commanded, who does not desire a reward, making everything a means to Allah. Its sign is not seeing one's deed, and it is known by fear and by not turning toward seeking reward, and by shame before Him, because he sees that he has not fulfilled the right of the Master as it should be fulfilled, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿They give what they give while their hearts are fearful that they will return to their Lord﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 60]. Al-Qushayri said: [It is said]: sincerity is purifying the deed from defect. Al-Razi said: sincerity is the pure intention, because [the intention] is lasting, whereas the deed ends, and the deed needs the intention, while the intention does not need the deed. And because the expression by the noun (*ism*) conveys establishment and steadfastness, He emphasized it by His saying: ﴿upright (hunafa')﴾, meaning in the utmost inclination (p-194) together with the evidence toward the truth, such that there is no crookedness in them at all. Rather, whenever any slight deviation occurs, they present it to the evidence and incline with it by their natural inclination (*hanaf*), which leads them to righteousness, so they become in the utmost uprightness. This is the worship of excellence (*ihsan*). The root meaning of *hanaf* in the language is inclination. Al-Malawi said: custom has restricted it to inclination toward good, and for this reason al-Ahnaf ibn Qays was so named because of an inclination in his legs inward from the front to the back. They called inclination toward evil *ilhad* (deviation). So the *hanif* in the absolute sense is one who disavows the roots of the five religions: the Jews, the Christians, the Sabians, the Magians and the polytheists; and their branches, from all sects to the true beliefs; and their consequences, from sins and misdeeds to righteous action, which is the station of piety (*taqwa*); and [he disavows] the disliked matters to the recommended ones, which is the first station of abstinence (*wara'*); and [he disavows] superfluities out of compassion for the creatures of Allah, which is what does not concern one, to what concerns one; and this is the second station of abstinence; and what leads to superfluities, which is the station of asceticism (*zuhd*). Thus the verse comprises both stations of sincerity: one of them looks to the Truth, and the second looks to creation. Sincerity belongs to the station of one occupied with purifying himself for Him, because it is singling out the Truth with intention in obedience; and fear belongs to the station of one occupied with purifying himself from Him, because it is turning away from all created beings toward Allah the Exalted and toward what pleases Him.

(p-195) When He mentioned the root of religion, He followed it with the branches, beginning with the greatest of them, which is the gathering point of religion and the place of detachment from obstacles. So He said: ﴿and establish﴾, meaning they make it upright without any crookedness whatsoever, with all its conditions, pillars and limits, ﴿the prayer (salah)﴾, so that by this it becomes fit to stand by itself, and it is the glorification of the command of Allah the Exalted.

When He mentioned the connection to the Creator, He followed it with the connection to creation, so He said: ﴿and give the zakat﴾, [meaning] by bringing it to those who deserve it, out of compassion for the creatures of Allah, as help in religion. But they distorted that and altered it by their crooked natures. According to the people of Allah, zakat includes all that Allah has provided of intellect, hearing, sight, tongue, hand, foot, standing, and other things, as is clear from His saying: ﴿and from what We have provided them they spend﴾ [al-Anfal: 3].

Since this is a good and clear religion, [but] they turned away from it in favor of the evidences they had, He increased their rebuke by praising it, so He said: ﴿And that﴾, meaning and the situation is that this described worship in the stated manner, which is at the utmost height and goodness, ﴿is the religion of the upright (al-qayyimah)﴾, meaning the religion (*millah*), or the souls, or the books in which there is no crookedness. On the first reading, it is the attribute-to-qualified construction (*idafah* of the qualified to the qualifier). It is reported from al-Khalil ibn Ahmad that he said: it is the plural of *qayyim*, and *qayyim* and *qa'im* (one who stands) are one, and the meaning is the religion of those who stand for Allah the Exalted in monotheism. It indicates what you had estimated regarding the matter of the polytheists, by their mention in the result of what passed (p-196) in His saying, emphasizing for the sake of rejecting them:

﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve﴾ — that is, there occurred from them the veiling of their minds' perception after it had been turned toward correct reflection, so they went astray and persisted in that, even if they were not deeply rooted in it. ﴿From among the People of the Book﴾ — that is, the Jews and the Christians — ﴿and the polytheists﴾ — that is, those deeply rooted in polytheism. By the use here of the descriptive term, and of the verb in ﴿those﴾ [i.e., in the earlier verse, ﴿أُولَئِكَ﴾ / "those"], — and God knows best — it indicates that the polytheist turns back from his polytheism and believes if he was not deeply rooted in polytheism, unlike the People of the Book: whenever any one of them becomes entangled in disbelief, he does not turn back from it, even if his entanglement with it is in the weakest of its forms. The same applies to everyone who is attributed to knowledge, especially if he is dull, whenever a doubt presents itself to him after he has turned back from it. Therefore He gathered them together in His saying: ﴿in the Fire of Hell﴾ — that is, the Fire which meets them with scowling and frowning, shall be a punishment to their bodies — ﴿abiding therein﴾ — that is, on the Day of Resurrection, or in the present state, because of their striving toward its causes. The sharing of the two groups in the genus of punishment does not necessitate equality in its type; rather, it varies according to the intensity or lightness of the disbelief.

Since the greater part of the context concerns worship and encouragement toward it — recitation, prostration, and disengagement from disbelief — He did not mention eternity by its explicit wording, but was content with what indicates it, and said, as a conclusion to what has passed: ﴿Those﴾ — that is, the far-removed, the hateful — ﴿they﴾ — that is, specifically, by what their hearts contain of corruption — ﴿are the worst of creation﴾ — that is, the creatures who neglected the reform of their souls and fell short in their needs and aims. And this is a fire for their spirits when it is proclaimed against them.

When he had mentioned the enemies and begun with them, because the context is to censure those who clung stubbornly to the familiar and abandoned the known good, he followed them with the allies (*awliya'*, the friends of God), saying, emphasizing against the denial of the disbelievers: ﴿Indeed, those who believe﴾, i.e., who acknowledged faith from all of creation, the angels and others, ﴿and do righteous deeds﴾, i.e., as confirmation of their faith, ﴿righteous deeds﴾, i.e., this category (of deeds). Since the bliss of the heart is greater, he placed it before the bliss of the body, for the sake of intensifying their praise, and said: ﴿Those﴾, i.e., those of the highest ranks, ﴿they﴾, i.e., exclusively, ﴿are the best of creation﴾.

Since He had singled them out for excellence, He mentioned their reward, saying, mentioning the paradise of their bodies and magnifying it for them by expressing His bounty to them with the word "reward" (jaza'), which signals that it is a recompense for what they were described with: ﴿Their reward﴾, that is, for their acts of obedience. He magnified it with His saying: ﴿with their Lord﴾, the One who nurtures them and is good to them, ﴿gardens of Eden﴾, that is, a dwelling they will never leave, ﴿beneath which rivers flow﴾, that is, flowing continuously without interruption. Since the general presence of water would prevent complete enjoyment, He restricted it with His saying: ﴿beneath them﴾, that is, beneath their ground, their chambers and their trees, ﴿the rivers﴾.

Since enjoyment is not complete except with permanence, He said: ﴿abiding therein forever﴾. Since in this context looking at the encouragement [to good] is more effective in urging adherence to the known proof and departure from familiar custom, He emphasized the meaning of eternity to magnify their reward with His saying: ﴿forever﴾.

Since all of this is the fruit of contentment, and stating it explicitly is more pleasing to the eye, because it is the paradise of the spirit, He said, resuming or giving the reason: ﴿Allah is pleased﴾, that is, by what He possesses of the attributes of majesty and beauty, ﴿with them﴾, that is, by what had preceded for them of care and success. Since contentment, when it comes from both sides, is more complete and higher for them, He said: ﴿and they are pleased with Him﴾, because no wish remains for them except that He has granted it to them, along with their knowledge that He is bountiful in all of that, that nothing is obligatory for Him toward anyone, and that no one can estimate Him as He deserves. Were He to take people to account by what they deserve, He would destroy them. The greatest of His blessings upon them is what He bestowed upon them of following the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), for that was the cause of every good.

Since that might be claimed to belong only to specific people in a specific time, He generalized it and drew attention to the quality that was the cause of their deeds, which were the cause of their reward, saying: ﴿That﴾, that is, this exalted matter by which they were recompensed, ﴿is for him who fears his Lord﴾, that is, who fears the One who is good to him with a fear befitting Him, so he does not incline to procrastination and laziness, nor does he habituate himself to evil by following desire in indulging in what is forbidden, but rather he is among those (p-199) who seek the lofty qualities of character, consulting his heart about what pleases his Lord. Thus the continual succession of His favors increases him in fear, and that increases him in gratitude, for fear is the essence of the matter and the impetus toward every good, and it belongs to those who have gnosis (ma'rifah). Al-Malawi said, in substance: when a person senses a punishment coming to him or a loss, a state befalls him called fear (khawf), which is the heart being dislodged from the tranquility of security, and its unease and agitation from anticipating something hateful. If it intensifies it is called wajal (anxious dread), because of its wandering within the soul; if it intensifies further it is called rahab (awe-fear), because it leads to flight. This is the state of the believers who flee to God. And whoever is overcome by love, through being absorbed in witnessing the beauties, is befallen by a state called mahabah (reverent love), for he is never free of fear of distance or rejection due to heedlessness or abasement. And whoever is overcome by veneration, through being absorbed in witnessing the majesties, enters into awe (ijlal). Beyond this fear lies

﴿Only those of His servants who have knowledge fear Allah﴾ [Fatir: 28]. Whoever fears his Lord with this fear is freed from everything in himself that is unfitting for His sublime presence, does not deviate from clear evidence nor waver concerning it, and fear never leaves a heart without ruining it. Thus it is fit to cast doubt on everything that leads to building up [the self]. The end of the surah has returned to its beginning in this regard, and in dividing people into two categories: a category freed from the caprice of its own soul, which saved it, and a category that remained in its captivity, which destroyed it.

I have mentioned in "Masa'id al-Nazar li'l-Ishraf 'ala Maqasid al-Suwar" the secret of the Prophet (ﷺ) singling out Ubayy (may Allah be pleased with him) to recite this surah to him specifically. Its summary is (p-200) that the reason for singling him out was that he found two of the Companions (may Allah be pleased with them) disagreeing with him in the recitation, so he brought them both to the Prophet (ﷺ), who ordered them, and they recited to him, and it pleased him. He said: "Then denial entered my soul more intensely than it had in the Jahiliyyah. The Prophet (ﷺ) struck my chest, and I broke into sweat, and it was as though I were looking at Allah in awe." Then he related to me the account of the lightening (of the recitation) through the seven ahruf (modes). The surah in which the disagreement occurred was al-Nahl, and in it is that Allah will raise His Messenger (ﷺ) on the Day of Resurrection as a witness, that the Book was revealed to him as an explanation of everything, guidance and mercy, that the Holy Spirit was sent down to him with the truth to make firm those who believe, and that the Jews disagreed about the Sabbath. The surah "Lam yakun," despite its brevity, comprehensively contains in summary all that is in al-Nahl in its length, with an addition. In it is a warning against doubt after clarification, and a condemnation of the state of one who does that, and that his state will be like that of the disbelievers among the People of the Book in obstinacy, so he will be the worst of creation. The Prophet (ﷺ) recited it to him [ʿalayhi] (may Allah be pleased with him) as a reminder of all of this, in a manner more eloquent and concise, so that it would be quicker for him to grasp, more firmly fixed in the soul, more steadfast in the heart, and more beloved to his nature. Allah therefore singled him out for steadfastness and willed him to remain firm. He became among those who are desired and who are drawn by Allah to what his heart reached, through the blessing of the Prophet's (ﷺ) striking of his chest: from the unveiling of veils, the negation of devils, the gazing upon the sacred radiances (p-201), and witnessing that sublime presence. His state came to be that he became the most purified of the Companions (may Allah be pleased with them) in vigilant attention to the Prophet's (ﷺ) recitation, through what he recalled of the noble matter by his being singled out for it. So whenever he recited this comprehensive surah, he would be absent from his own recitation, listening with the ears of his heart to the Spirit of Prophethood reciting it to him, and thus the state of witnessing that he attained by the secret of that strike remained with him.

Because of his firmness in this station, the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The best reciter among you is Ubayy." Related by Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi and Ibn Majah from Anas (may Allah be pleased with him), and it is sound, though some related it as mursal. Among what is in it, which I did not mention in the Masa'id, is the Sunnah of humility, lest anyone be prevented by what he sees of his own high rank from reciting to one who is below him, for what prevented most of the People of the Book from embracing Islam was only their seeing what they had of knowledge of the books of Allah and the traditions of the Messengers, peace be upon them, and the Arabs' ignorance of that. They looked at what had been and did not look at the present condition. Envy shaved away their religion and stripped them of their faith, and they became the most wretched of people, as He pointed out at the beginning of the surah. We ask Allah for pardon and well-being in religion, in this world and the next. Amin.
